title: Ionic oxides and a hardened metal

stimulus.title: Two oxides and a metal
stimulus.html:
A materials lab compares two ionic oxides and a metal used to make a cutting tool.

Data for three solids
SubstanceIons or atoms (radius, pm)Melts at (°C)
SrOSr²⁺ (118), O²⁻ (140)2531
BaOBa²⁺ (135), O²⁻ (140)1923
Iron, FeFe atom (126)1538

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why SrO melts at a higher temperature than BaO. Your answer should refer to both compounds.

rubric.point: Same ion charges (2+ and 2−) in both; Sr²⁺ is smaller than Ba²⁺, so the cation-anion distance is shorter in SrO and the Coulombic attraction (lattice energy) is greater, so more energy is needed to melt it
accept: the charges are the same but Sr²⁺ (118 pm) is smaller than Ba²⁺ (135 pm), so the ions are closer and attract more strongly
Coulomb's law: same q₁q₂, smaller r for SrO, so stronger attraction

parts.sample: Both compounds contain a 2+ cation and the O²⁻ anion, so the charges are the same. Sr²⁺ (118 pm) is smaller than Ba²⁺ (135 pm), so the distance between the centers of the cation and the anion is shorter in SrO. By Coulomb's law the attraction between the ions is stronger in SrO, so more energy is needed to separate them, and SrO melts at a higher temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Solid SrO does not conduct electricity, but molten SrO does. Explain this difference in terms of the particles present.

rubric.point: Charge is carried by ions; in the solid the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice, while in the melt the ions are free to move
accept: the Sr²⁺ and O²⁻ ions can move when melted but are locked in the solid
mobile ions in the liquid carry the current

parts.sample: SrO is made of Sr²⁺ and O²⁻ ions. In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice, so they cannot move to carry charge. When SrO melts, the ions can move past each other, so they carry an electric current.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A small amount of carbon (atomic radius 77 pm) is added to iron to make steel. In the box, draw a particle diagram of steel showing at least 12 iron atoms and a few carbon atoms. Include a key.

rubric.point: Iron atoms drawn as larger, equal-size circles in a regular arrangement, with fewer, much smaller carbon circles in the spaces between them (not replacing iron atoms); key identifies both
accept: small C atoms in the gaps of an iron lattice

parts.sample: Rows of at least 12 large, equal circles labeled Fe, touching their neighbors, with three or four much smaller circles labeled C sitting in the spaces between groups of Fe atoms. Key: large circle = Fe atom, small circle = C atom.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Steel is harder and less malleable than pure iron. Explain why, using your diagram from part (c).

rubric.point: The carbon atoms in the interstitial spaces get in the way of the layers of iron atoms, so the layers cannot slide past each other as easily (less malleable, harder)
accept: the small carbon atoms pin the iron layers and stop them sliding
interstitial C atoms block the movement of layers of Fe

parts.sample: In pure iron, layers of Fe atoms can slide past each other while the delocalized electrons keep holding them together, so iron bends. In steel the small carbon atoms sit in the spaces between the Fe atoms, where they block the layers from sliding. The metal resists changing shape, so it is harder and less malleable.
